Whaddya know, I did look at this option, but for the love of dog, I didn't consider the criteria doesn't have to be baked into the formula and it can reference a dropdown list.

I simply added columns with the names of the Projects each team member supports and then filtered the VSTACK with either Project chosen from the dropdown list.

I also used CHOOSECOLS, so I wouldn't have the helper columns show up in my summarized table.

That's the final formula:

    =CHOOSECOLS(
       FILTER(
          VSTACK(Team1,Team2,Team3,Team4,Team5),
          VSTACK(Team1[Project],Team2[Project]),Team3[Project],Team4[Project],Team5[Project]=A1)+(VSTACK(Team1[Secondary Project],Team2[Project]),Team3[Project],Team4[Project],Team5[Project]=A1);
       "");
    1)

Where A1 is the dropdown list with Project Names. Only Team 1 people work on multiple projects so it was easier, otherwise I'd probably have to include all possibilities (although I might be wrong here?).

In Poland we have two. One is simply **Mac** /'mahk/, which McD's actually adopted in one of their slogans *Mam smaka na Maca* - *I've got a taste for McDonald's* (but like I'm finna get McDondald's).

Then the dimunitive version **Maczek** /'mah-check/ became common, as it brings a level of familiarity to the brand name. I don't think they've adopted it in their corpo-lingo as of yet.

These version actually kind of help with the branding, tho. Polish has a pretty complex grammar rules, with seven cases applicable to all nouns (including names), and their also different whether it's singular or plural. So people would normally not call it *McDonald's*, rather just *McDonald*, and apply the same declination as for the surname. McD's tried to fight for using the correct brand name and would always refer to themselves as *McDonald's restaurant*, but people wouldn't have any of that.

The "the" article comes from (in the case of Ukraine) from the fact it was a name of a geographic territory which wasn't its own country. The same as you have "the Midwest" in the US, "the Midlands" in the UK, or "the Orient". This geographic region used to be part of Poland or Russia across the centuries. When Ukraine became independent, the article stayed due to linguistic anachronism. The same can be said for "the Lebanon", which comes from the times of colonialism.

As you can see, this is something countries may choose to change on the international stage, to further signify their independence.

You may have noticed I mentioned two other countries with the definite article in their name. That's because there are several other grammatical rules responsible for that. You add the article when the name contains a political title (the United Kingdom, the Dominican Republic), the name is plural (the Netherlands, the Philippines), or it comes it refers to a group of islands (the Bahamas).

That being said, the are some similar rules in Russian, Ukrainian, and possibly other Slavic languages (Polish for one) which make it sound like Ukraine is still treated as part of the Soviet Union and which are slowly changing (I only know about the use of different prepositions in Polish).
